headline: South Africa and Rwanda lose their US trade deal.
summary: President Trump told Congress Monday he will drop South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA, which lets African countries sell goods in the US duty-free, from January 1. His trade office cited barriers to US trade, corruption in South Africa and human rights in Rwanda. South Africa sold $1.7 billion through it last year. Rwanda, $44 million.
cover_answer: Corruption, the US says, and backing rebels in Congo.
table_question: Should a country lose a deal for how it treats its own people?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The United States has a deal that lets countries in Africa send things like cars and fruit here without paying a fee at the border. On Monday the president said South Africa and Rwanda are out from January, like a club card at the shop that stops working. They can still sell here, it just costs more, and the grown-ups are talking.
5-7.why: A fee at the border is a thing they can picture. The club card makes the deal a card, not a law.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script makes the deal a club card that stops working, one they have seen a parent hand over at a till. Who was right is beyond this age; the script leaves it to the grown-ups. Expect "did they do something bad?" The US government thinks so. The two countries say no.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: AGOA is a US law from 2000: African countries that keep its rules sell goods here tax-free. Each year the US checks who still qualifies, like a referee checking boots at kick-off. This year South Africa failed on corruption and Rwanda on a war in Congo, so from January they pay the tax.
8-12.why: Rules, a yearly check, a fail. The referee is a check they have stood through.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults apply them fairly, so the script gives them the rule, the yearly check and the fail, in that order. A referee at kick-off is a check they have stood through, and it raises the question they will ask anyway: is the referee fair? Expect "so who decides?" The US trade office, once a year.

13-17.script: Should trade reward behaviour? The US says South Africa and Rwanda broke AGOA's rules, so from January their goods lose duty-free entry. South Africa says these issues were never in the talks. Second: a former US official says China and the EU don't switch trade on and off. Who pays more for that?
13-17.why: Two true things: the rules were there, and the US has fought both countries all year. Which drove it?
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: AGOA's rules have been there since 2000, and the US has fought with both governments for months over Congo and over white South Africans. The script hands them both and asks which drove the decision. Expect "isn't this just politics?" The rules are real and so is the fight. Let them argue.

5-7.q: Can they still send us things?
5-7.a: Yes. From January it just costs them more at the border.

8-12.a: Corruption, the US says, and Rwanda's army backing rebels in Congo.
South Africa most. It sold $1.7 billion through the deal last year.

13-17.q: Is this about trade or politics?
13-17.a: Both. The statement lists rules broken; the fight has run all year.
Greer says the US wants them to take the steps to qualify.
